biography.value:
Background

Thomas grew up just outside of Daggerford on a ranch, in a ranching family — not wealthy, but comfortable and well-respected. Some of the men in the family are a bit tall. A legend told within the family is that the name Invictus comes from a far-away land of humans and means "undefeated." His parents are still alive and are running the ranch.

Due to his early days living on a ranch, he is strong, he picked up common sign language, and has a way with animals. His father has an old longsword and a few old javelins that Thomas would practice with in his spare time. Every so often as a child, he would encounter an outlander wood elf wandering through the ranch, with whom he practiced communicating via sign language and in Elvish. They don't see each other often, but they have known each other since childhood. (That wood elf is Jetten Ellisedell.)

Thomas is naturally charismatic. He has always been drawn to the sacred. His true loves are learning and books, especially theology. His family's economic status allowed him to wander into town often and spend time in a monastery devoted to the god Lathander. He learned to read and write and became a scribe by the time he was a teenager, making a decent living apart from the ranch. Being well-read has given him deep insight into others' motivations.

Working as a scribe softened his body a bit — he is still strong, and when he can, he walks back to the ranch and helps his family with manual labor. But the reading has worn his eyesight, he's never been able to hold his alcohol, and the bookwork has left him less used to pain and discomfort than he once was. He has studied many maps and has learned quite a bit of arcana.

He married Ann when he was 17. Until six months ago, they lived in town. They had four children — three girls and a boy. She was not from a notable family.

As a scribe he was in high demand; his favorite clients were the local government and the monastery. Through this work he learned much about theology, law, contracts, maps, and the judicial system, and came to understand the importance of truth, justice, and moral behavior to a functioning society — though he sees that laws can be arbitrary, and can be broken sometimes in the service of higher ideals.

About two years ago, through copying various contracts and manifests, he began to suspect that a band of thieves was working in Daggerford to collect illegal contraband for sale to groups that practice necromancy. At first this was a curiosity he kept to himself. He kept paying attention. Eventually the evidence was too great to ignore. Naively assuming that most people are like him — devoted to the good — he brought his suspicions to the attention of the wrong town official. One day about six months ago, while he was in the monastery copying religious tomes, his wife and children were brutally tortured and murdered at home. Some body parts were left for him to see in the residence; others, he is quite sure, ended up being used for necromancy. He suspects a nearby cult of Shar and perhaps a nearby hag coven might be customers of body parts sold by the band of thieves. As part of these investigations, he pieced together information related to the existence of the Broken Heart.

He never thought about leaving town, and certainly not about becoming an adventurer. After the murders, he seeks vengeance and desires to expiate the world of evil and corruption. He has become a paladin devoted to these goals. The Broken Heart may or may not be connected to his personal tragedy — but given that a hag coven and a cult of Shar seem to hold two of the shards, he decided to make the quest for the Broken Heart his first adventure.

He is generally charismatic and gregarious, but he holds himself and others to high standards. His personal tragedy has left him edgy. Under the surface he hates what he perceives as lazy or childish behavior in others; there is a temper there that he keeps a tight lid on, and when tired or overwhelmed it can come out. He can be perceived as overly serious and sometimes Pharisaical — he understands this, but he doesn't feel that way on the inside.

A Devout Warrior of Sacred Oaths

Core Paladin Traits

Primary Ability

Strength and Charisma

Armor Training

Starting Equipment

Choose A or B: (A) @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.equipment.Item.phbarmChainMail0]{Chain Mail}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.equipment.Item.phbarmShield0000]{Shield}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.equipment.Item.phbwepLongsword0]{Longsword}, 6 @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.equipment.Item.phbwepJavelin000]{Javelins}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.equipment.Item.phbagHolySymbolV]{Holy Symbol}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.equipment.Item.phbagPriestsPack]{Priest’s Pack}, and [[/award 9GP]]; or (B) [[/award 150GP]]

Paladins are united by their oaths to stand against the forces of annihilation and corruption. Whether sworn before a god’s altar, in a sacred glade before nature spirits, or in a moment of desperation and grief with the dead as the only witnesses, a Paladin’s oath is a powerful bond. It is a source of power that turns a devout warrior into a blessed champion.

Paladins train to learn the skills of combat, mastering a variety of weapons and armor. Even so, their martial skills are secondary to the magical power they wield: power to heal the injured, smite their foes, and protect the helpless and those who fight at their side.

Almost by definition, the life of a Paladin is an adventuring life, for every Paladin lives on the front lines of the cosmic struggle against annihilation. Fighters are rare enough among the ranks of a world’s armies, but even fewer people can claim the calling of a Paladin. When they do receive the call, these blessed folk turn from their former occupations and take up arms and magic.

Becoming a Paladin …

As a Level 1 Character

  • Gain all the traits in the Core Paladin Traits table.
  • Gain the Paladin’s level 1 features, which are listed in the Paladin Features table.

As a Multiclass Character

  • Gain the following traits from the Core Paladin Traits table: Hit Point Die, proficiency with Martial weapons, and training with Light and Medium armor and Shields.
  • Gain the Paladin’s level 1 features, which are listed in the Paladin Features table. See the multiclassing rules in chapter 2 to determine your available spell slots.

Breaking Your Oath

A Paladin tries to hold to the highest standards of conduct, but even the most dedicated are fallible. Sometimes a Paladin transgresses their oath.

A Paladin who has broken a vow typically seeks absolution, spending an all-night vigil as a sign of penitence or undertaking a fast. After a rite of forgiveness, the Paladin starts fresh.

If your Paladin unrepentantly violates their oath, talk to your DM. Your Paladin should probably take a more appropriate subclass or even abandon the class and adopt another one.

Found throughout the multiverse, humans are as varied as they are numerous, and they endeavor to achieve as much as they can in the years they are given. Their ambition and resourcefulness are commended, respected, and feared on many worlds.

Humans are as diverse in appearance as the people of Earth, and they have many gods. Scholars dispute the origin of humanity, but one of the earliest known human gatherings is said to have occurred in Sigil, the torus-shaped city at the center of the multiverse and the place where the Common language was born. From there, humans could have spread to every part of the multiverse, bringing the City of Doors’ cosmopolitanism with them.

Human Traits

Creature Type: Humanoid

Size: Medium (about 4–7 feet tall) or Small (about 2–4 feet tall), chosen when you select this species

Speed: 30 feet

As a Human, you have these special traits.

Resourceful. You gain Heroic Inspiration whenever you finish a Long Rest.

Skillful. You gain proficiency in one skill of your choice.

Versatile. You gain an Origin feat of your choice (see chapter 5). Skilled is recommended.

A silver sun-disk of Lathander, the Morninglord, its rays worked in rose-gold — the dawn that ends every night. It was given to Thomas by the brothers of the Daggerford monastery where he learned his letters, and he inked its inner band himself in a scribe's flawless hand: "Every wound closed is a page saved."

He holds it as his spellcasting focus, and habitually rubs its edge with his thumb before a hard decision — the way another man might pray aloud.

You speak a one-word command to a creature you can see within range. The target must succeed on a Wisdom saving throw or follow the command on its next turn. Choose the command from these options:

Approach. The target moves toward you by the shortest and most direct route, ending its turn if it moves within 5 feet of you.

Drop. The target drops whatever it is holding and then ends its turn.

Flee. The target spends its turn moving away from you by the fastest available means.

Grovel. The target has the Prone condition and then ends its turn.

Halt. On its turn, the target doesn’t move and takes no action or Bonus Action.

Using a Higher-Level Spell Slot. You can affect one additional creature for each spell slot level above 1.
Until the spell ends, your attacks with weapons deal an extra 1d4 Radiant damage on a hit.

A fine silver-nibbed quill, its shaft worn smooth to the exact grip of one hand. A gift from the elder copyist of Daggerford's monastery of Lathander, given the day Thomas first earned a scribe's wage with it. The old brother said only: "Write nothing you would not sign."

A palm-sized book of Lathander's dawn-prayers, copied out in Thomas's own immaculate hand at the monastery where he learned his letters. The margins carry tiny, scrupulous corrections to the older text it was copied from — an error preserved is an error twice told.
A heavy brass seal ring cut with a personal cipher — a quill crossed over a sword. Pressed into hot wax, it marks a letter as genuine to anyone who knows the hand behind it.

A heavy silver key stamped with the gauntlet sigil of the Silver Gauntlet Tavern, hung on a braided leather fob marked Suite Four. It opens the tavern's four-room suite at the west end of the house — and the iron-bound treasury door that adjoins it, kept locked at all hours. Behind that door is the strongroom where Daggerford's adventurers store what they can't afford to lose.

The party's own travel chest sits inside, packed and waiting for the road.

A silver scroll-case charm cast in the form of Oghma's blank scroll — the page on which all that is known has yet to be written. It came to Thomas through his scribe's trade, not his temple: a loremaster of the Binder pressed it into his hand years ago, in thanks for a ruined archive restored line by patient line. "The Morninglord has your mornings," the old scholar said. "Give the Binder your ink."

Thomas has carried it ever since alongside his sun-disk — the dawn and the written word, the two faiths of his two lives.

A stoppered clay vial of bitter green cordial, found among the web-wrapped effects of a traveller who never left the temple. The label, in a tidy, careful hand, reads only: “One swallow, seventh-day, as ever. — Selma.”

Whoever drinks a swallow sleeps utterly without dreams for the next seven nights. No apothecary could name any other virtue in it — nor say why anyone would brew such a thing, or take it as ever.

Wondrous Item, Uncommon

It belonged to an eladrin knight-errant who never left the temple. The lantern was forged in the Feywild and knows its kin: hooded, its glow strips the invisible bare within thirty feet. She hangs in the webs unnaturally shriveled, a husk with the life drunk out of it, the lantern still shuttered at her belt — whatever the wisps showed her, she never thought to look at it honestly.

While lit, this hooded lantern burns for 6 hours on 1 pint of oil, shedding Bright Light in a 30-foot radius and Dim Light for an additional 30 feet. &Reference[Invisible apply=false] creatures and objects are visible as long as they are in the lantern’s Bright Light. You can take a Utilize action to lower the hood, reducing the lantern’s light to Dim Light in a 5-foot radius.

The blade that was First Light. The rose-gold has run to ink; the steel drinks the candlelight and gives none of it back. It is not cold. It is simply without dawn.

Consecrated once to the Morninglord and surrendered in a sunless temple, this longsword now belongs to the Lady of Loss. The warmth left it the way a door closes somewhere far off — no thunderclap, no wrath: withdrawal. Its bearer knows the sword's name the way he knows his own reflection.

Potion, Uncommon

After drinking this potion, you can take a Bonus Action to exhale fire at a target within 30 feet of yourself. The target makes a DC 13 Dexterity saving throw, taking 4d6 Fire damage on a failed save or half as much damage on a successful one. The effect ends after you exhale the fire three times or when 1 hour has passed.

This potion’s orange liquid flickers, and smoke fills the top of the container and wafts out whenever it is opened.

A quarter of a heart, turned to crystal: venom green, bright and vivid and faintly poisonous-looking, the size of two cupped hands, with the chambering and the sheared-off vessels still there inside the stone like flaws in a gem. It is warm — warmer than the air — and it beats, slowly, faintly, the light inside it moving out through the facets with every beat. It does not chip and it does not scratch. It has already been broken.

It is the exact green of the dragon that hoards it, which is either a coincidence or isn't — and the Wyrmwood has grown briar around it the way a body grows scar tissue.

The vision. The Thornheart requires attunement. The first time you hold it, it shows you one thing. A beautiful green woman, glowing white, leaves crowning her head, weeping. She closes her hands over her own chest, and her heart bursts. The pieces scatter into the dark, hardening as they fly. The burst drives the mists back in a great ring, baring a bare green valley next to a beautiful lake. Where she stood, a tree: grey, leafless, asleep. A single faint heartbeat, and it is over.

While you carry the Thornheart you have advantage on Dexterity saving throws.

Once between dawns, you can press the shard to the breast of a body dead no more than ten days: green light threads down through it like new roots taking hold, and it casts raise dead — the shard is the only component needed.

It is one chamber of a heart — and a heart has four. You cannot shake the feeling that, whole, it could do so much more.
